name: tree-sitter
description: Rust bindings to the incremental, error-tolerant parsing library used by editors

license.comment: Workspace Cargo.toml: `license = "MIT"`, inherited by the `tree-sitter` lib crate; crates.io reports MIT.

approach.comment: README: "a parser generator tool and an incremental parsing library". Grammars are written in `grammar.js`, compiled by the CLI to C, and driven by the incremental runtime the Rust crate wraps. Dual by the same logic RESEARCH.md applies to rust-sitter.

implementation.comment: `build.rs` compiles the C11 runtime `lib/src/lib.c` via `cc`; Cargo.toml declares `links = "tree-sitter"`. Grammar crates (`tree-sitter-rust` etc.) likewise compile generated `parser.c` with `cc`.

crates-io.comment: Runtime crate. Companion crates: `tree-sitter-language` (Language type shared with grammar crates), `tree-sitter-highlight`, `tree-sitter-tags`, `tree-sitter-loader`, and the `tree-sitter-cli` generator.

documentation.comment: Official guide (Using Parsers, Creating Parsers, Queries, Syntax Highlighting); API reference at docs.rs/tree-sitter.

first-release.comment: crates.io `created_at` 2018-05-18. The oldest version still listed on the versions endpoint is 0.17.1 (2020-11-03); earlier releases are no longer listed.

latest-stable-version.comment: Checked 2026-09-19; published 2026-08-30. Research reflects tree-sitter 0.27.0 (the 0.26.x line, last 0.26.13 on 2026-08-23, had MSRV 1.77). master is already at 0.28.0-dev.

grammar-class.comment: Docs: "Tree-sitter is based on the GLR parsing algorithm. This means that while it can handle any context-free grammar, it works most efficiently with a class of context-free grammars called LR(1) Grammars."

grammar-definition.comment: Grammar is a JavaScript DSL in `grammar.js`, compiled by `tree-sitter generate` to `src/parser.c`; the Rust crate consumes the compiled `Language`, not the grammar.

left-recursion.comment: LR/GLR tables: left-recursive rules (e.g. `binary_expression: $.expression '+' $.expression` with `prec.left`) are the documented norm. Per Assessment Guidelines LR generators get `native`.

ambiguity-handling.comment: Unresolved LR(1) conflicts fail `tree-sitter generate` unless resolved with `prec`/`prec.left`/`prec.right`; conflicts listed in the grammar's `conflicts` field are instead explored by GLR ("we want the parser to explore both possibilities"), with `prec.dynamic` picking the surviving parse rather than returning a forest.

backtracking.comment: Deterministic table-driven LR; ambiguity is handled by GLR stack forking, not by backtracking.

lexer-integration.comment: Context-aware lexer generated from the grammar's token rules and `extras`; custom tokenisation via an optional external scanner written in C. No external token stream can be fed in.

precedence-pratt-support.comment: `prec(n, ...)`, `prec.left`, `prec.right`, and `prec.dynamic` in the grammar DSL — the grammar-level precedence/associativity facility analogous to LALRPOP `%left`/`%right`.

unicode-aware.comment: Input may be UTF-8 or UTF-16 (LE/BE) or a custom encoding via a `Decode` trait; the lexer operates on code points and grammar regexes match Unicode.

input-types.comment: `Parser::parse` takes `impl AsRef<[u8]>` (so `&str`, `&[u8]`, `Vec<u8>`); `parse_with_options` takes a `FnMut(byte_offset, Point) -> chunk` callback intended for "piece tables, ropes, or other custom formats"; `parse_utf16_le/be` take `&[u16]`. Tokens cannot be supplied.

streaming-partial-input.comment: The read callback is pulled on demand until it returns an empty chunk (EOF); there is no "need more input" result. Parsing can be cancelled via a progress callback but not resumed. Incremental reparse of an edited buffer is a different capability (see Incremental Reparsing).

zero-copy.comment: `Node<'tree>` is a `Copy` handle into the tree; `Node::utf8_text(&source)` returns a `&str` slice of the caller's source without allocating. The tree itself is heap-allocated by the C runtime and does not store source text.

span-tracking.comment: Every node exposes `start_byte`/`end_byte`/`byte_range` and `start_position`/`end_position` as `Point { row, column }` (0-based, column in bytes); `Range` bundles both.

output-model.comment: Produces a concrete syntax tree with a node "for every individual token in the source code, including things like commas and parentheses"; nodes are untyped (`kind()` strings, optional field names), comments are `is_extra` nodes, whitespace is implied by byte-range gaps. No typed AST is built.

semantic-actions.comment: No actions in the grammar; users walk the tree afterwards with `TreeCursor`/`Node::children` or run `Query`/`QueryCursor` patterns over it.

whitespace-comment-handling.comment: Grammar `extras` (default whitespace; typically also comments) may appear anywhere without being mentioned in rules; named extras such as comments are kept in the tree and flagged via `Node::is_extra`.

stateful-parsing.comment: No user state is threaded through the parse from Rust; context-sensitive lexing (indentation, heredocs) must be implemented in a C external scanner that owns its own serialisable state.

error-recovery.comment: Built-in, non-configurable repair: unrecognised input becomes `ERROR` nodes ("parts of the code that could not be incorporated into a valid syntax tree") and zero-width `MISSING` nodes are "inserted by the parser in order to recover from certain kinds of syntax errors". README: "Robust enough to provide useful results even in the presence of syntax errors".

multiple-errors-per-parse.comment: A single parse always yields a full tree; any number of `ERROR`/`MISSING` nodes can be present and located via `has_error`, `is_error`, `is_missing`, or `(ERROR)`/`(MISSING)` query patterns.

expected-token-reporting.comment: `ERROR` nodes carry no expected set. A `MISSING` node names the single token the parser inserted, and `Language::lookahead_iterator(state)` lets the user enumerate symbols valid in a parse state (via `Node::parse_state`), but this must be assembled by hand rather than being reported on the error.

custom-error-types.comment: Parsing never returns an error type — syntax errors live in the tree as nodes. The only error types (`LanguageError`, `QueryError`, `IncludedRangesError`) are fixed setup errors, not substitutable.

error-span-fidelity.comment: Every `ERROR`/`MISSING` node has a precise byte range and row/column `Point`s (4 per guideline). No labels or secondary spans, and no message text at all — the caller must synthesise diagnostics.

diagnostic-crate-integration.comment: No first-party or documented bridge to ariadne/miette/codespan-reporting/annotate-snippets; consumers map `Node::range()` into whichever reporter they use.

contextual-error-messages.comment: The grammar DSL has no way to attach labels or expectations to rules, and error nodes carry only kind and span.

incremental-reparsing.comment: `Tree::edit(&InputEdit)` adjusts node ranges, then `Parser::parse(text, Some(&old_tree))` produces a new tree that "internally shares structure with the old tree"; `Tree::changed_ranges` reports what changed.

lossless-syntax-tree.comment: Concrete syntax tree with every token (including punctuation) and comments as `extra` nodes; whitespace is not stored as nodes but is recoverable from the byte-range gaps against the original text, which the tree does not own. RESEARCH.md names tree-sitter as the reference `true`.

syntax-highlighting-queries.comment: S-expression query language (`Query`/`QueryCursor` in the Rust API) plus the `highlights.scm`/`locals.scm`/`injections.scm` convention and the first-party `tree-sitter-highlight` and `tree-sitter-tags` crates; docs note the highlighter is used on GitHub.com.

used-by-lsp-ide.comment: Zed depends on the `tree-sitter` crate directly (git-pinned). Helix uses the same C runtime through its own `tree-house`/`tree-house-bindings` crates rather than this crate. Neovim (C) links the C library: "Nvim integrates the `tree-sitter` library for incremental parsing of buffers". rust-analyzer does not use it.

runtime-speed-tier.comment: Maintainer benchmark with a hand-written competitor: tree-sitter-rust README reports initial parse of a 2,157-line file at 6.48 ms vs rustc's own parser, "around two to three times as long as rustc's hand-written parser" — i.e. the 1.5–3x `fast` band. Incremental re-parse after an edit is quoted at under a millisecond. Checked 2026-09-19.

compile-time-impact.comment: No measured build-time delta found. The runtime crate is a small C file compiled once via `cc`; the real cost is per grammar crate, whose generated `parser.c` can reach multi-megabyte sizes (issue #1041: 25 MB for Zig, 8.7 MB for TypeScript), but no timings were published. Left `null` per guideline.

allocation-strategy.comment: Subtrees are heap-allocated, reference-counted objects in the C runtime (tree copy is "incrementing an atomic reference count"; incremental parses share unchanged subtrees). Rust-side `Node` handles are `Copy` and allocation-free, but the allocator is not user-controllable.

generated-code-size.comment: Generated `parser.c` parse tables are routinely multi-megabyte: 8.7 MB for TypeScript and 25 MB for Zig reported in issue #1041 (closed as not planned).

no-std-support.comment: `#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]` with `extern crate alloc` (needs `alloc`); `default-features = false` drops `std`. CI runs `cargo check --no-default-features` per target. The C runtime still needs a libc/allocator at link time.

unsafe-usage.comment: Thin bindings over the C API: roughly 80+ `unsafe` blocks/functions, no `forbid(unsafe_code)`; optional `bindgen` feature regenerates the FFI declarations.

proc-macro-reliance.comment: No proc-macro crates in the dependency list; grammars are compiled C, not macros.

build-rs-step.comment: The crate's own `build.rs` compiles the C runtime with `cc`, and every grammar crate (`tree-sitter-rust`, ...) has a `build.rs` compiling its generated `parser.c` (+ `scanner.c`). Users pulling published grammar crates write no build script themselves; users authoring a grammar do.

dependency-count.comment: Non-optional: `regex` (default-features off), `streaming-iterator`, `tree-sitter-language`. Optional: `wasmtime-c-api-impl` (feature `wasm`). Build-deps: `cc`, `serde_json`, optional `bindgen`. Checked at 0.27.0.

wasm-compatible.comment: `wasm32-unknown-unknown` is in the CI matrix; `build.rs` has a dedicated `configure_wasm_build()` path using the wasm stdlib headers shipped by `tree-sitter-language` (`DEP_TREE_SITTER_LANGUAGE_WASM_HEADERS`). A C compiler able to target wasm32 (clang) is still required, and `Send`/`Sync` impls are gated off on `target_family = "wasm"`.

async-friendly.comment: `Parser`, `Tree`, and `Language` are `Send + Sync` (non-wasm targets); trees are cheaply cloned via atomic refcount for cross-thread use. The read callback itself is synchronous, so async sources must be materialised or chunked before parsing.

github-stars.comment: Rounded figure shown on the GitHub repo page ("27k"), checked 2026-09-19; ~2.9k forks.

crates-io-downloads.comment: ~39.5 M all-time (14.6 M recent) for the `tree-sitter` crate, checked 2026-09-19.

maintenance-status.comment: Five releases between 2026-06-28 and 2026-08-30 (0.26.10 → 0.27.0); master already carries 0.28.0-dev. Note Helix maintains its own bindings (`tree-house-bindings`) to the same C runtime rather than using this crate.

documentation-quality.comment: Long-form official guide (using parsers, creating parsers, queries, highlighting) plus README examples; docs.rs API reference is only ~60% documented and much of the guide is written against the C API. No migration guides. 4 per guideline.

tutorial-book.comment: The tree-sitter.github.io guide is a multi-chapter book covering grammar authoring, parsing, queries, and highlighting.

notable-users.value: Zed, Neovim, Helix (via tree-house bindings), GitHub.com code navigation/highlighting
notable-users.comment: Zed depends on the Rust crate; Neovim embeds the C library; Helix wraps the C runtime with its own bindings; the syntax-highlighting docs state `tree-sitter-highlight` is used on GitHub.com.

bus-factor.comment: Hosted under the `tree-sitter` GitHub organisation with a `core` team; crate owners are Max Brunsfeld (Zed) and Amaan Qureshi plus the org team. Day-to-day maintenance is concentrated in those two, so the effective bus factor is closer to a small team despite the org structure.
